Even though it seems especially corrupt, this is actually a really common outlook on early company performance for start-ups. The idea comes from Eric Reis's "MVP," or minimum viable product. You just want to get what's required out immediately, and then iterate over it and fix issues as they arise. Recently, this outlook has shifted from being functionality-focused to appearance-focused. So, it doesn't matter if your start-up product is buggy, as along as it looks good and sounds good to investors. It's this way of thinking that excuses things like fudging numbers -- it's a kind of "growth hack" that is seemingly innocuous and can have a big payoff. I don't mean to justify it, it's definitely a very shitty way to do business, and indicates a profound lack of personal character. Just saying that this is a common philosophy in the valley.
